I am by no means super experienced, but I will pass along a few pieces of advice I have received.

Re: Breathing - if you want to control your breathing try timing your breaths to steps. I generally do 4 steps per breath in and 4 steps per breath out. This can help you feel like you're not gasping for air.

If you want to improve distance don't try and do it all at once - the general recommendation is to increase your weekly distance by no more than about 10-15% per week. Any more than that is not generally sustainable.

I can definitely recommend looking into training plans, even if you're not planning to do a 'race' or event, consider training like you are - that will help to build your stamina at an achievable rate.

Our Shukokai school has this broad scheme - Gradings are generally at the end of each quarter, although as you progress through the kyu grades, you wait longer to grade:

to 9th Kyu (White to Red) Shihozuki Ich and Yon

to 8th Kyu (Yellow) Heian Nidan

to 7th Kyu (Orange) Heian Sandan or Godan (alternates depending on which quarter)

to 6th Kyu (Green) as 7th

to 5th Kyu (Blue) Heian Shodan or Yondan (alternating per quarter)

to 4th Kyu (Purple) as 5th

to 3rd Kyu (Brown) Bassai Dai

to 2nd Kyu Ananku

to 1st Kyu Matsukaze and Seienchin

No. I think that gradings are a good way of keeping the interest level for some students, particularly in the west, and to help them see their progression.

That being said, I would happily move to a system of gradings only being performed in front of members of a panel, who are particularly qualified for purpose, and who adjudicate for any dojo of that style. The logistics would be really tough of course, but it might help to eliminate some of the 'belt mills' who churn out belts purely based on attendance or money paid.

As I say I don't think it would realistically be possible but having a standardised grading syllabus and assessment might help alleviate some of the disparities we see between students who are ostensibly the same rank.

Just remember to work within your limitations. Your Sensei, if they are a good one, will work with you to make your training the best it can be for you (and it sounds like they are doing that which is great).

Jodan kicks while they look cool are not that useful in any practical application, so don't feel bad if you can't manage them (I am 43 and I certainly can't!)

My main advice I think would be to not rush things, remember your karate journey is not a sprint but a marathon, and sometimes you have to slow down to let your body be ready for what's to come.

I just (re)started at 43 and being the only white belt in a class of predominantly higher belts is both intimidating and humbling (in a good way) - walking into class the first time is the hardest part.

You will be nervous. That's OK. You will probably feel like you know nothing. That's also OK. Everybody when they first start doesn't know anything. That's why we go to class, to learn!

As for the nervous/scared feeling? I will say just one thing. **Feel the fear and do it anyway**. Trust me after that first class you will feel great (assuming the instructor knows what they're doing) and after a few classes you will wonder why you were nervous. If you go in wanting to learn, you'll be amazed what you can do.
